## Overview

Energy storage technologies, store energy either as electricity or heat/cold, so it can be used at a later time. Wider deployment and the commercialisation of new battery storage technologies has led to rapid cost reductions, notably for lithium-ion batteries, but also for high-temperature sodium-sulphur (“NAS”) and so-called “flow” batteries. # Falling Battery Storage Costs Are Quietly Reshaping Electricity Markets

Featuring  Christian Kaps. By Rachel Layne on January 23, 2026

Rising electricity prices will likely spur more people to embrace battery systems that store solar power, says research by **Christian Kaps**. Do governments still need to offer incentives?

Sustainability and self-reliance motivated early adopters of solar energy and battery storage in Germany. Now, falling costs—and rising electricity prices—could compel more people to pull back from the grid.

As solar panel and battery prices drop, research by Harvard Business School Assistant Professor Christian Kaps predicts some 54% of German households would benefit from using a solar-battery combination. The rise of self-generated electricity would have major implications for German utilities and the country’s power grid, which gets a substantial, yet decreasing share of energy from fossil fuels.

Incentives and subsidies helped drive $807 billion in renewal energy investment globally in 2024 alone, as part of efforts to confront climate change. With electricity costs surging in many parts of the world, Germans stand to become producers and consumers of power in one of the most advanced clean-energy economies—even without such enticements.

> In many European countries, at least in many markets with higher electricity prices, solar and storage is going to be a profitable investment.

“In many European countries, at least in many markets with higher electricity prices, solar and storage is going to be a profitable investment,” says Kaps, coauthor of “Residential Battery Storage—Reshaping the Way We Do Electricity” with Serguei Netessine, a professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. The article is forthcoming in the journal *Operations Research*.

The shift wouldn’t be without consequences. Researchers predict that increased solar and storage adoption in Germany would reduce residential electricity demand by 38%, cutting utilities’ revenue. Rising generation and delivery costs could also challenge the industry’s pay-per-use model.

## Rapid adoption, dizzying change

Since the early 2000s, solar panel prices have dropped 85%, the authors note. And the cost of lithium-ion batteries has dropped by nearly 90% during the decade until 2020. The trend helped spur a 20-fold increase in German household battery systems between 2015 and 2020.

As more households use battery storage, it becomes harder for utilities to predict how much electricity to generate and send to the grid—and when to do it. Demand from homes with battery-solar setups can drop to near zero when it’s sunny outside, but spike during cold, dark days that deplete home storage. It’s unlikely that most households will be totally self-sufficient and leave the larger electricity grid completely, the researchers write.

## Why Germans turned to storage

Kaps and Netessine analyzed solar-storage adoption from 2018 through 2020, using data from 3,200 households served by the German firm Solarwatt. Back then, batteries cost almost twice as much as today, but consumers who installed them prioritized self-sufficiency and the potential to slash climate-damaging emissions, motives the authors call “nonmarket valuation.” The change cost households a median 29 euro cents (34 cents in the US) more per kilowatt hour than relying on the power grid.

“It was really this idea of, ‘I'm producing solar power myself. I want to use more of that myself,’” Kaps says. “It's a sustainability argument. Germany has a long history of debating how to generate electricity.”

Paradoxically, early adopters of battery-and-solar systems used 4% more electricity and lifted overall carbon emissions slightly as they sold less solar energy back to the grid. The authors show how batteries, which enable users to save their power for less sunny times, will be key to leveraging renewable energy in the future.

## A ‘tipping point’ for storage adoption?

Kaps and Netessine tested scenarios to gauge not only German solar and battery adoption in 2025 but also the implications for both utilities and the power grid. Their analysis assumes:

* No subsidies for solar or batteries, though the researchers also evaluated the impact of tariffs and rebates.
* Solar panel and battery prices that declined 22% and 25%, respectively, between 2025 and 2020.
* Electricity prices of 38 euro cents per kilowatt hour.

Their model predicts that—unlike the early adopters from 2018-2020 they studied—costs, rather than a desire for sustainability or independence, will motivate the next wave of adopters.

“Residential adoption of this technology in markets with expensive electricity is close to a technology tipping point,” the authors write. “Investment decisions are most sensitive to assumptions on the decrease in storage cost, followed by a moderate sensitivity to the price of electricity.”

## Consequences for the power market

A 38% decline in households’ grid demand could create challenges for one of the more reliable—and expensive—electricity systems in the world. With such a drop, the traditional model of volume-based pricing—one rate per kilowatt hour used—might become unsustainable, the authors write.

Utilities will also need to be nimbler and more responsive to the volatile needs of solar-and-storage households, who save by using stored energy on low-demand days but then double their use on high-demand days. For example, utilities could add gas-burning turbines for peak times or install their own huge batteries to quickly meet fluctuations.

> The big change for policymakers is thinking about the fact that now individuals can make their own generation—and even strategic consumption—decisions with batteries.

Kaps says policymakers might also need to intervene to maintain stability for utilities by:

* **Supporting flexible pricing.** Such rules would let utilities charge higher prices during peak times. Alternatively, utilities could charge higher fixed fees each month to cover grid costs and reduce volume-related fees.
* **Incentivizing storage adoption, not solar.** Policymakers may encourage households to store their solar energy and time their discharge, rather than just subsidizing its generation as solar becomes increasingly abundant.
* **Adding parameters to subsidies in key areas.** Capping cumulative reimbursement by household or region would still encourage adoption in areas with low solar-battery use.

“The big change for policymakers is thinking about the fact that now individuals can make their own generation—and even strategic consumption—decisions with batteries,” Kaps says. “So, the classic one- or two-tier electricity tariff and straight subsidies may have possibly unintended consequences.”

# The Age of Battery Storage–Part I: Resilient, Repositioned and Increasingly Essential to the U.S. Power System and American Energy Dominance

The passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) in 2025 reshaped the policy environment for U.S. clean energy generation and infrastructure. While the legislation accelerated the phase-out of several tax incentives for renewable generation, utility scale-battery energy storage systems (BESS) emerged from the policy overhaul relatively intact. Standalone and co-located BESS sited with solar, wind and other generation resources as hybrid facilities will remain eligible for the life of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 48E investment tax credit (ITC) through 2035, preserving a critical financing mechanism for developers and investors even as incentives for wind and solar tightened.

This policy continuity has positioned battery storage as one of the relative “winners” in the aftermath of the OBBBA’s curtailment of clean energy tax incentives. Continued eligibility for the ITC allows projects to continue to access tax equity financing structures that historically supported traditional solar, wind and hybrid facilities but that are increasingly being adapted to storage assets. As a result, the sector retains important access to a source of capital support at a time when the broader clean energy policy landscape is becoming more restrictive.

Market data reflects the strong momentum that storage has built in recent years. According to the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence’s Energy Storage Market Outlook Q1 2026 report, U.S. battery storage deployments reached approximately 57 gigawatt hours (GWh), or 28 gigawatts (GWs), in 2025, representing a 29% year-over-year increase. Utility scale installations accounted for nearly 50 GWh of this total, with California, Texas and Arizona representing roughly 74% of capacity additions, according to SEIA. Their forecasts suggest continued growth, with installations projected to reach roughly 70 GWh in 2026, representing approximately $25 billion in capital investment.

Despite these strong fundamentals, the outlook for the sector is neither unequivocally bullish nor bearish. Battery storage faces a complex set of countervailing forces, but strong underlying demand for grid flexibility and capacity is reinforcing the technology’s role in the power system, particularly as rapid load growth from data centers and electrification accelerates. At the same time, new foreign entity of concern (FEOC) restrictions under the OBBBA, tariff volatility affecting battery supply chains and persistent interconnection and permitting constraints are introducing new uncertainties. Taken together, these forces suggest the U.S. storage market may experience a period of adjustment in the near term, even as the long-term role of battery storage in the power system becomes increasingly integral and resilient.

This blog is the first in a two-part series examining the evolving role of battery storage in the U.S. power sector. Part 1 analyzes the near-term headwinds shaping the industry, including new FEOC supply chain restrictions, tariffs and trade policy, permitting and interconnection constraints, and tightening capital markets. Part 2 will examine the structural demand drivers, technological innovation and evolving market and regulatory frameworks that are expected to sustain battery storage deployment and reinforce its role as a core component of the modern electric grid.

Deployment Momentum is Real, but a Near-Term Contraction May Follow

Recent deployment data shows the scale and speed at which the U.S. storage market has expanded. Utility-scale battery installations have increased dramatically over the past several years, with cumulative installations continuing to climb. Rapid growth in installations over the past several years reflects the increasing role that storage plays in balancing variable renewable generation, providing ancillary services and meeting peak demand.

However, forecasts for deployment diverge across major research organizations, reflecting uncertainty around policy implementation, supply chain restructuring and project economics.

As illustrated in the chart above, BloombergNEF and industry forecasts project materially different growth trajectories for the U.S. battery storage market. BloombergNEF projects installations rising to approximately 48 GWh in 2026, in contrast to the SEIA forecast anticipating deployments reaching around 70 GWh in the same year. The divergence highlights the uncertainty surrounding the outlook for BESS as developers navigate the new supply chain restrictions, trade policies and financing conditions.

Looking further ahead, forecasts also diverge on the longer-term trajectory. BloombergNEF projects annual U.S. installations reaching roughly 80 GWh by 2030, while the SEIA-Benchmark forecast suggest deployment could approach 110 GWh annually by the end of the decade.

While the magnitude of these projections differs, both outlooks point to continued expansion of the U.S. battery storage market. The question facing developers and investors is less whether the sector will grow than how quickly that growth will occur.

Recent global market analysis suggests that the United States may experience a short-term adjustment period before the next phase of expansion. Wood Mackenzie’s 2026 outlook, Five Trends to Look For in Global Energy Storage in 2026, notes that while global storage installations exceeded 100 GWs for the first time in 2025, the U.S. market is likely to experience a temporary slowdown in the near term, 2026 through 2027, as supply chains adapt to new policy constraints and trade dynamics.

Several factors are contributing to this potential near-term contraction:

* FEOC restrictions: New OBBBA rules are forcing developers to restructure battery supply chains to remain eligible for tax credits, potentially constraining supply and raising costs until domestic or allied manufacturing scales.
* Trade policy barriers and volatility: Tariffs and shifting trade actions are increasing cost uncertainty and complicating project timelines.
* Permitting, interconnection delays and market rules: Lengthy queues, slow approval processes and ill-adapted power market retail regulations remain major barriers to deploying new storage capacity.
* Tighter capital markets: Higher uncertainty and financing costs are pushing developers to prioritize only the most economically and regulatory‑certain projects.

Importantly, these headwinds primarily affect the pace of deployment rather than the underlying demand for storage capacity. Structural drivers for battery deployment remain strong. Electricity demand in the U.S. is growing after decades of relative stagnation, driven in part by electrification, industrial reshoring and the rapid expansion of data centers. Grid operators increasingly require flexible resources capable of responding quickly to fluctuations in supply and demand, particularly as renewable generation continues to grow.

In this context, battery storage is emerging as a core component of modern grid infrastructure rather than a supplemental technology tied exclusively to renewable energy generation. Even under more conservative deployment scenarios, analysts expect storage capacity to continue expanding significantly over the next decade.

As a result, the near-term slowdown anticipated in some forecasts should be understood as a market adjustment period rather than a structural decline. As supply chains reorganize to comply with new policy requirements and domestic manufacturing capacity expands, the sector is likely to return to a stronger growth trajectory later in the decade.

The divergence in current forecasts ultimately reflects the complexity of the transition now underway. Battery storage remains one of the fastest-growing segments of the energy sector, but the path forward will depend heavily on how quickly developers, manufacturers and policymakers adapt to the evolving policy and supply chain landscape shaping the U.S. power system.

## FEOC Restrictions Introduce a New Supply Chain Constraint

Among the most consequential policy changes introduced by the OBBBA are the FEOC restrictions governing supply chains for clean energy technologies. These rules restrict tax credit eligibility for projects using equipment sourced from certain foreign-linked entities, particularly those connected to China.

For battery storage developers, FEOC compliance presents a significant challenge. Much of the global battery manufacturing ecosystem, particularly lithium-iron-phosphate cell production, is currently concentrated among Chinese manufacturers which are now prohibited entities. The OBBBA goes so far as to ban six specific companies and their successors, five of which, according to Intertek CEA’s 2025 Q3 Energy Storage System Supply, Technology, and Policy Report, controlled 73% of the global energy storage market through 2024.

As a result, developers must restructure procurement strategies to maintain eligibility for federal tax incentives. This transition will take time. As Wood Mackenzie notes, many markets within the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) lack sufficient alternative manufacturing capacity to fully replace Chinese battery supply in the near term.

Industry analysts note that this shift is likely to result in a bifurcation of supply chains. On one side are FEOC-compliant supply chains relying on domestic or allied manufacturing, which may carry higher costs in the near term. On the other side are lower-cost battery supply chains linked to Chinese manufacturers that may be excluded from projects seeking federal incentives.

The development of domestic manufacturing capacity is underway, but scaling these facilities to meet market demand, even with the IRC Section 45X incentive still in place, will likely take several years.

## Tariffs and Trade Policy Add Further Uncertainty

Trade policies are also reshaping the economics of battery storage projects. A complex mix of trade initiatives and tariff regimes to address country-by-country trade deficits and alleged unfair market practices are affecting battery modules, components and materials, including semiconductors, critical minerals and structural materials. These actions have collectively introduced significant additional volatility into procurement strategies, equipment pricing and project development timelines.

Projects that do not intend to rely on tax credits directly or tax equity financing and so are not restricted by FEOC requirements must still contend with tariffs on imports from China, which controls an overwhelming majority of battery manufacturing capacity at 80%. They must also endure national security tariffs on specific materials and technologies. Those complying with FEOC and so more heavily restricted with respect to sourcing from China, must still endure the latter tariffs intended to combat trade agreement violations, economic imbalances and the alleged unfair market practices.

### Updated Section 301 Tariffs on Battery Supply Chains

One of the most consequential structural changes affecting battery supply chains is the continuation and modification of Section 301 tariffs on Chinese imports following the U.S. Trade Representative’s 2024 four-year review determination. These updates expanded tariffs across strategic clean-energy and advanced technology sectors affecting roughly $18 billion in imports from China, including batteries, battery components, semiconductors and critical minerals.

The review concluded in 2024, and implementation of tariff increases began that same year with staggered timelines. Tariffs on lithium-ion batteries used in non-electric vehicle applications, including stationary energy storage systems, are scheduled to rise to 25% beginning in 2026.

The determination also targets upstream battery materials. Tariffs on certain critical minerals used in battery and semiconductor supply chains increased to 25% beginning in 2024, while tariffs on natural graphite, a critical lithium-ion battery anode material, will increase to 25% beginning in 2026.

Additional tariff increases affect supporting technologies. Tariffs on semiconductors, essential components of battery management systems, inverters and grid-control electronics, are scheduled to increase to 50% beginning in 2025, raising the cost of key electronics used in energy storage systems.

### Section 232 Tariffs on Battery and Structural Materials

BESS are also indirectly exposed to Section 232 tariffs on a variety of input materials and semiconductors.

Steel and aluminum are embedded throughout utility-scale energy projects, including containers/enclosures, racking and mounting, fencing, and certain balance-of-plant and interconnection hardware. The energy sector largely relies on imports of specific types of steel in particular, including those that can withstand extreme temperatures and pressures. Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminum, which were already in place prior to these actions but have been modified in recent years and are currently set at 50%, can therefore raise all-in installed costs for storage developers and engineering, procurement and construction contractors.

Section 232 has increasingly served as a mechanism for the administration to impose tariff-based trade restrictions on imports viewed as threatening U.S. resources and manufacturing. This year, the administration initiated several industry-relevant Section 232 cases covering semi-finished copper products, processed critical minerals and semiconductors. The investigations have concluded, resulting in a 50% tariff on copper, 25% on semiconductors, and ongoing monitoring and negotiations on processed minerals.

The steel and aluminum, copper, and semiconductor actions also extend to certain derivative and related products. In the case of steel and aluminum, industry participants may nominate additional derivatives for inclusion on the tariff list.

U.S. Department of Commerce (DOC) antidumping and countervailing duty (AD/CVD) trade actions have also been focused on upstream battery materials. In a recently concluded investigation covering active anode material (AAM) imported from China, DOC initially issued a final affirmative determination finding that Chinese producers dumped and subsidized these materials.

While DOC clarified that completed BESS containers, both utility-scale and residential, were excluded, raw active anode material, battery cells and battery modules fell within the scope of the investigation. Though the International Trade Commission ultimately decided in a 2-1 vote March 12 that imports of active anode material from China are not materially impeding the domestic industry, had the determination been affirmative, domestic battery manufacturers would have been additionally impacted by the proposed duties. It is possible that other alternative tariff mechanisms, such as Section 232, will be pursued for the same purpose in the future.

### Supreme Court Reversal of IEEPA Tariffs, Interim Section 122 and Section 301

In early 2025, the administration also imposed sweeping tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that applied broadly to imports from China, Mexico and other countries. These tariffs significantly disrupted global supply chains economy wide and contributed to elevated costs across the clean energy sector, including battery manufacturing and storage projects.

However, in February 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that IEEPA does not authorize the president to impose tariffs under its policies, striking down the broad regime. Despite the repeal, the IEEPA tariffs, established through multiple executive actions, have already made a significant contribution to the overall impact of tariffs on the battery industry that will have lingering effects even as the duties are phased out. Several solar and energy storage firms have already begun legal proceedings for refunds on duties on the estimated $168 billion to 182 billion collected under IEEPA as of February 2026. Canadian Solar, JA Solar, Jinko Solar, Longi and Trina Solar filed complaints with the U.S. Court of International Trade (CIT). Automaker BYD Co. Ltd. also filed a lawsuit in the CIT challenging the tariffs through four of its U.S. subsidiaries: BYD America; BYD Coach and Bus; BYD Energy; and BYD Motors.

The administration has attempted to partially replace the broader tariff regime using other trade authorities. In February 2026, the president issued a proclamation imposing a temporary 10% global import surcharge under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, citing balance-of-payments concerns. The surcharge applies to most imported goods for a period of 150 days effective Feb. 24, 2026, although several categories of products, including certain critical minerals and goods already subject to Section 232 tariffs, are excluded. Section 122 allows for a maximum of 15% to be applied, should the president decide the rate is necessary.

The administration and the United States Trade Representative also announced new broad Section 301 investigations into 15 countries and the European Union regarding structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors and 60 countries regarding alleged failures to impose and effectively enforce prohibitions on the importation of goods produced with forced labor. New Section 301 rates can then effectively replace the universal but temporary Section 122 rate in the long run.

Taken together, these overlapping tariff regimes and trade investigations are accelerating the realignment of battery supply chains toward domestic and allied manufacturing. However, they have also created significant cost and availability uncertainty in the near term for battery storage developers. For projects seeking to qualify for the Section 48E ITC, trade compliance, FEOC compliance and procurement strategy are increasingly intertwined, complicating project development and financing decisions.

These policy objectives align with broader industrial policy goals, including the expansion of domestic manufacturing, which the Section 45X advanced manufacturing tax incentive was intended to support. Over time, this combination of trade policy and industrial incentives could create a more robust domestic battery supply chain and substantial global alternatives to countries and companies subject to FEOC.

But in the near term, trade policy tariffs and the transition may increase costs and introduce project delays as developers adjust to new sourcing requirements.

## Permitting, Interconnection, Market Constraints Continue to Slow Deployment

Beyond trade policy, physical infrastructure bottlenecks remain a major constraint on battery storage deployment. Across U.S. power markets, permitting and interconnection delays continue to slow the pace at which new projects can reach construction.

Interconnection queues in many regional transmission organizations (RTOs) and independent system operators (ISOs) have grown dramatically in recent years as developers have proposed thousands of gigawatts of new renewable energy generation and storage capacity. In some markets, projects may wait several years to complete interconnection studies and secure grid connection agreements.

Battery storage projects face many of the same procedural hurdles as generation projects, even though their operational characteristics can provide flexibility benefits to the grid. Battery storage facilities must go through the same process for interconnection as do direct resource to electricity generation facilities like solar and wind, even if they are independent of a primary generation resource such as wind and solar, long queues and study delays continue to push battery storage project timelines further into the future as well.

Permitting challenges also persist. While battery projects generally face fewer siting conflicts than large generation facilities, they can still trigger environmental reviews, local land-use approvals and transmission upgrades. Federal permitting requirements and required upgrades affecting associated transmission infrastructure can further delay projects, particularly in regions where renewable and storage development overlaps with federal lands or sensitive environmental areas.

In regions such as PJM, the Midcontent Independent System Operator (MISO) and the Southwest Power Pool (SPP), batteries have also been stymied by market rules that do not fully recognize, or properly pay for, their flexibility. Unlike the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) (where real-time prices reward fast response) and the California Independent System Operator (CAISO), regulators that provide compensation for a broad set of grid services), PJM’s rules currently penalize batteries for responding to real-time grid needs if that response conflicts with a pre-scheduled commitment in another time window. That limits batteries’ ability to “stack” revenues (arbitrage, capacity/resource adequacy, ancillary services) and reduces the economic case for deploying them at scale. MISO has historically undervalued storage as well.

As a result, permitting, interconnection and market processes and protocols increasingly represent one of the most significant non-economic barriers to expanding storage capacity in the United States.

## Capital Markets Are Adjusting to Policy and Market Uncertainty

The evolving policy landscape has also affected the financing environment for battery storage projects. As regulatory uncertainty has increased and supply chain risks have grown more complex, investors and lenders have become more cautious in underwriting new projects.

Historically, renewable energy development experienced a seesaw of policy frameworks for tax incentives. Consistent ebbs and flows that were stabilized by the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) which created a more robust tax equity market. The policy changes introduced by the OBBBA, particularly the complex FEOC regime, combined with uncertain and heavily burdensome trade policy, have again destabilized certainty and increased perceived project risk for many investors.

As a result, capital markets are becoming more selective, prioritizing projects with strong counterparties, secure supply chains and well-defined revenue structures. Developers that cannot clearly demonstrate compliance with FEOC requirements or secure reliable equipment supply may face more difficulty obtaining financing.

Rising interest rates and greater exposure to volatile, short-term “merchant” revenues are straining traditional financing models for battery storage, especially because storage typically lacks the long-term PPAs that stabilize solar and wind cash flows. Storage projects economics often rely on multiple and often unpredictable revenue streams from capacity markets, energy arbitrage or ancillary services rather than fixed power purchase agreements. Lenders and investors also view batteries as higher-risk due to limited operating history, as well as uncertainty around degradation and long-run performance, resulting in tougher terms, higher equity requirements, and constrained debt (for example, ERCOT standalone storage often supports only approximately 20%-30% debt). These capital constraints are pushing many developers toward “develop and flip” strategies rather than long-term ownership, while policy uncertainty, despite IRA tax credit transferability boosting liquidity, adds additional risk.

Together, these factors have made financing more difficult for some projects and have reinforced a broader shift toward greater investor risk aversion. In the near term, this dynamic may slow project development as developers and investors reassess risk tolerance and mitigations and project structures.

## A Period of Adjustment, Long-term Growth and Transformation

Taken together, the policy, trade and financing developments shaping the battery storage sector point to a period of adjustment rather than decline. New FEOC compliance requirements are forcing supply chain restructuring while tariffs and trade actions are increasing cost uncertainty. All the while, permitting and interconnection bottlenecks continue to delay projects and capital markets are becoming more selective as investors reassess risk in a more complex policy environment. These headwinds are likely to slow the pace of deployment in the near term, particularly for projects with uncertain supply chains, merchant revenue exposure or interconnection risk.

Yet these challenges do not change the underlying role that battery storage is beginning to play in the U.S. power system. Instead, they are reshaping how projects are financed, where supply chains are located and how developers structure projects to manage risk. In many ways, the current moment represents a transition from the early, policy-driven phase of battery deployment to a more mature market in which storage must compete, operate and be financed as core infrastructure.

Part 2 of this blog series will examine the other side of this transition: the structural demand drivers, technological innovation and evolving market structures that are expected to sustain battery storage deployment even as policy and market conditions become more complex. While the near-term outlook may be defined by adjustment and uncertainty, the long-term outlook will be defined by necessity.
